questiontext.text: What do we count when we analyze the time complexity of a solution?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Seconds depend on the machine, but the number of operations as n grows describes how the solution scales on any machine.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The number of basic operations as a function of the input size n
The number of seconds it takes on our own computer
The number of lines in the source code
The size of the compiled file

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 100, steps = 0;
while (n > 1) {
    n /= 2;
    steps++;
}
cout << steps << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Integer division gives 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, so the loop divides six times. The count is about log2(100).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What is the Big-O form of 3n² + 5n + 7 operations?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Big-O ignores constants and keeps only the fastest-growing term, so 3n² + 5n + 7 simplifies to O(n²).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 6, cnt = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
        cnt++;
    }
}
cout << cnt << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The inner loop starts after i, so it counts each pair once: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 15, which is n(n-1)/2. It is still O(n²).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: A problem says n can be as large as 200000. Which complexity is the safe choice?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. With about 10⁸ operations per second, n² would need 4·10¹⁰ operations. n log n is only a few million, so it passes comfortably.

name.text: Q07 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operator into the gap so the loop runs about log n times (it should print 10 for n = 1024).

main.cpp
int n = 1024, steps = 0;
for (int x = n; x > 1; x [[1]] 2) {
    steps++;
}
cout << steps << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Dividing x by 2 each turn reaches 1 after log2(n) = 10 turns. Subtracting 2 would need about 512 turns, and multiplying would never end.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int n = 1024, steps = 0;
for (int x = n; x > 1; x /= 2) {
    steps++;
}
cout << steps << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each complexity with a typical example.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

O(1)  →  [[1]]

O(log n)  →  [[2]]

O(n)  →  [[3]]

O(n log n)  →  [[4]]

O(n²)  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Recognizing these five patterns lets you estimate most solutions at a glance.

The correct answer:

  • O(1) → Reading v[i] from a vector
  • O(log n) → Binary search or a lookup in a set
  • O(n) → One loop over all the elements
  • O(n log n) → Sorting with sort
  • O(n²) → Two nested loops over n

questiontext.text:
Sort each operation on a vector<int> v (n elements): constant time or linear time?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

v[i]  →  [[1]]

v.size()  →  [[1]]

v.push_back(x) (on average)  →  [[1]]

v.insert(v.begin(), x)  →  [[2]]

looping over all elements  →  [[2]]

v.erase(v.begin())  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Reading, the size and adding at the end are fast. Inserting or erasing at the front shifts all the other elements, which costs O(n).

The correct answer:

Constant time: v[i], v.size(), v.push_back(x) (on average)
Linear time: v.insert(v.begin(), x), looping over all elements, v.erase(v.begin())

cout << 1000000LL * sizeof(int) / 1000000 << " MB" << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. An int takes 4 bytes, so a million of them take 4 million bytes, which is 4 megabytes.

questiontext.text: Roughly how much memory does an array of 10 million int values need?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. 10⁷ values × 4 bytes = 4·10⁷ bytes, which is about 40 megabytes. That fits easily in a typical 256 MB limit.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
long long n = 100000;
cout << n * n << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A hundred thousand squared is ten billion, 10¹⁰. That is why a loop nested inside another loop of this size is far too slow.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What does "worst case" mean in complexity analysis?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. We describe the most work any input of a given size can cause, so that the solution is safe even on the hardest tests.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The largest number of operations the solution may need for an input of size n
The input that makes the program crash
The slowest computer that may run the program
The case where the answer is wrong

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 5, cnt = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    cnt++;
}
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        cnt++;
    }
}
cout << cnt << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The first loop adds 5 and the nested loops add 25, so the total is 30. For large n only the n² part matters, so the whole code is O(n²).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Why does v.insert(v.begin(), x) inside a loop of n turns make the solution O(n²)?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Each insertion costs about the current size of the vector, so n insertions cost 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is about n²/2.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Every insertion at the front shifts all the existing elements
Because the vector doubles its size every time
Because the loop runs n² times

name.text: Q16 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Complete the inner loop so each pair is counted once and the program prints 10 for n = 5.

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
int n = 5, cnt = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = [[1]]; j < n; j++) {
        cnt++;
    }
}
cout << cnt << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Starting at i + 1 counts only the pairs with i < j, which is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Starting at 0 would give 25 and starting at i would give 15.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int n = 5, cnt = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
        cnt++;
    }
}
cout << cnt << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

TLE  →  [[1]]

Big-O  →  [[2]]

Worst case  →  [[3]]

Amortized  →  [[4]]

Space complexity  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These terms appear in every discussion of efficiency, so make sure you can say each of them in your own words.

The correct answer:

  • TLE → Verdict: the program did not finish in time
  • Big-O → A symbol that summarizes growth of operations
  • Worst case → The most work any input of size n can cause
  • Amortized → Cost averaged over a sequence of operations
  • Space complexity → How much memory the program needs

questiontext.text:
Sort each loop: does it run about log n times or about n times?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)  →  [[2]]

for (int x = n; x > 1; x /= 2)  →  [[1]]

for (int x = 1; x < n; x *= 2)  →  [[1]]

for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2)  →  [[2]]

while (n > 0) n /= 10;  →  [[1]]

for (int i = n; i > 0; i--)  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Loops that multiply or divide the variable shrink the remaining work geometrically, so they are logarithmic. Loops that add or subtract a fixed amount walk through all n values, and a constant such as 2 does not change O(n).

The correct answer:

O(log n): for (int x = n; x > 1; x /= 2), for (int x = 1; x < n; x *= 2), while (n > 0) n /= 10;
O(n): for (int i = 0; i < n; i++), for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 2), for (int i = n; i > 0; i--)

questiontext.text: For very large n, which statement is true?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The logarithm grows very slowly (about 20 for a million), while n itself grows a million times. So n log n beats n² easily.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: An O(n log n) algorithm is much faster than an O(n²) algorithm
An O(n²) algorithm is faster because it has no logarithm
Both always take the same time
The faster one depends on the compiler only
